title: The House of David, Before and After the Exile
summary: The chapter lists the sons born to David in Hebron and in Jerusalem, then traces the kings of Judah from Solomon to Josiah and Josiah's sons. It follows the royal line through Jeconiah, the king taken captive to Babylon, to Zerubbabel and on for several generations after the exile.
story: Chapter 2 traced Judah's families down to David. Now the Chronicler gives David's own family, and this chapter is the spine of the book's hope. In a few verses it passes over four centuries: every king who sat on David's throne from Solomon to the last kings before the fall of Jerusalem. Then, where Kings ends with the exile, this list keeps going. Jeconiah is called the captive, but his line doesn't end in Babylon. It runs through Shealtiel and Zerubbabel, who led the returned exiles in rebuilding the temple, and on to men who lived in the Chronicler's own time. For readers without a king, this was quiet but powerful evidence: David's house still existed. God's promise to David, which chapter 17 will tell in full, had not been cancelled by the exile.
historical:
David reigned about forty years, roughly 1010 to 970 BC by common reckoning, seven and a half in Hebron over Judah and thirty-three in Jerusalem over all Israel (verse 4, as in 2 Samuel 5:5). The kings in verses 10 to 14 ruled Judah from Solomon's death around 930 BC until Josiah died in 609 BC. The list gives only the sons of David who reigned and so passes over Queen Athaliah, who seized the throne for about six years (2 Kings 11), since she was not a descendant of David.

Josiah's sons in verse 15 include Shallum, known in Kings as Jehoahaz (compare Jeremiah 22:11), who reigned only three months in 609 BC before Egypt deposed him. Jehoiakim ruled until about 598 BC. His son Jeconiah, also called Jehoiachin and Coniah, was taken to Babylon in 597 BC after a reign of three months, and Zedekiah reigned until Jerusalem fell in 587 or 586 BC. Jeconiah lived on in Babylon, and 2 Kings 25:27-30 records his release from prison under Nebuchadnezzar's successor. Clay tablets found in Babylon, listing rations for royal dependents, mention Jehoiachin king of Judah and his sons, a rare outside witness to the exiled royal family. Zerubbabel governed Judah around 520 BC and led the rebuilding of the temple (Ezra 3; Haggai 1). Hattush of verse 22 may be the descendant of David who returned with Ezra (Ezra 8:2).
cultural:
Royal households in the ancient Near East were large. Kings married for alliance as well as affection, and the mothers of David's first sons show it: Maacah was the daughter of Talmai, king of Geshur, a small kingdom north-east of the Sea of Galilee, and the marriage tied David to a neighboring royal house. The sons of concubines (verse 9) were legitimate members of the household but usually had lower standing in matters of inheritance. Because a king's mother mattered to the succession, the list carefully names each son's mother.

In the Hebrew text of verse 5 Bathsheba's name is spelled Bath-shua (the BSB gives the familiar form), and her father is Ammiel; in 2 Samuel 11:3 she is Bathsheba daughter of Eliam, and the two forms of her father's name use the same elements in reverse order. The Chronicler names Solomon last of her four sons, a reminder that he was not the obvious heir. The names in the later generations carry the faith of the people: Hasadiah means the LORD is kind, and Jushab-hesed means kindness will be returned. Families in exile named their children after the hope they held.
literary: The chapter has three parts. Verses 1 to 9 list David's sons by place of birth, Hebron and then Jerusalem, and close with a mention of his daughter Tamar. Verses 10 to 16 give the kings in a steady chain, each linked by the words his son, until the chain breaks under the pressure of the last years before the exile, when brothers and an uncle succeed one another. Verses 17 to 24 then pick up the line after the captivity. The rhythm of the middle section is almost like a drumbeat, and the reader feels how long the line lasted. The final section, with its more tangled branches, reads like a family record kept by people still waiting.

Sons born to David in Jerusalem
The kings of Judah from Solomon to Zedekiah
The line of Jeconiah after the exile

doctrines.note: The list is a witness to God's covenant with David. The Chronicler traces David's descendants past the exile to show that the house God promised to establish had not been destroyed, even when its throne was empty.
By ending not with the fall of Jerusalem but with living descendants of David, the chapter gives its readers a reason to wait. The promise has a future because the family still stands.
The royal line passes through war, murder, exile, and prison, yet it continues. The chapter quietly shows God keeping his word through centuries of human failure.

words.note: Assir, prisoner or captive, the title given to Jeconiah in verse 17. It marks the low point of the royal line: David's heir in a Babylonian prison. Yet the verse continues with his descendants, so the word stands at a turning point rather than an ending.

Zerubbabel, a Babylonian name usually taken to mean seed of Babylon or offspring of Babylon. He was born in exile and returned to lead the rebuilding of the temple. The prophet Haggai spoke of him as God's chosen signet ring (Haggai 2:23), reversing the judgment on his grandfather in Jeremiah 22:24.
Solomon, from the root of shalom, peace. His name fits the role the Chronicler gives him: the king of rest whose peaceful reign allows the temple to be built, as David will explain in chapter 22.

christ: This chapter is the Old Testament record behind the middle and last sections of Matthew's genealogy of Jesus. Matthew 1:6-12 follows the kings from Solomon to Jeconiah and then goes on to Shealtiel and Zerubbabel, just as these verses do, before continuing with names not found here. Luke 3:31 traces Jesus through Nathan, another son of Bath-shua listed in verse 5. Both Gospels are saying the same thing in different ways: Jesus is the son of David in whom the promise of this family line comes to rest. The Chronicler recorded a royal family with no throne and many generations of waiting. The New Testament announces that the heir has come. The chapter itself makes no prediction, but it keeps the line and the hope visible until he does.

hard.q: Who was Zerubbabel's father, Pedaiah or Shealtiel?
hard.a: First Chronicles 3:19 names Zerubbabel as a son of Pedaiah, while Ezra 3:2, Haggai 1:1, and Matthew 1:12 call him the son of Shealtiel. Pedaiah and Shealtiel were brothers, both sons of Jeconiah (verses 17 and 18). Interpreters have offered a few explanations. One is a levirate marriage: if Shealtiel died without a son, his brother Pedaiah may have married the widow, and the child would legally count as Shealtiel's (the custom is described in Deuteronomy 25:5-6). Another is that Pedaiah was the natural father and Zerubbabel was raised or adopted as Shealtiel's heir, perhaps as the next in the royal line. Some also note that the Greek translation of Chronicles reads Shealtiel here. Whatever the explanation, all the sources agree that Zerubbabel was Jeconiah's grandson and belonged to the house of David.

questions: The first readers of this chapter had no king but could still name David's descendants. What promises of God do you hold onto when you can't yet see them fulfilled?
Jeconiah is called the captive, and yet his line continues. How might God be at work in a season that looks like the end of something?
Exiled families named their children for kindness and hope. What do the names, words, and habits of your household say about what you believe?
